slot.brief: Compare ionic, covalent and interstitial hydrides via multiple statements (reducing nature, thermal stability, reaction with water); ask which set is correct, touching H2O2 stability as distractor.

stem:
Consider the following statements about hydrides:
I. Ionic hydrides react with water to liberate $\text{H}_2$, with $\text{H}^-$ acting as a reducing agent.
II. For group 16 covalent hydrides, thermal stability decreases and reducing character increases down the group.
III. Interstitial hydrides are generally non-stoichiometric and retain metallic conductivity.
IV. $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ is thermally more stable than $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Which statements are correct?

verdicts.working: I–III are correct: ionic hydrides release H₂ as H⁻ is oxidized; group 16 hydride stability decreases and reducing character increases down the group; interstitial hydrides are generally non-stoichiometric and retain metallic conductivity. IV is false because H₂O₂ is less thermally stable than H₂O.

working:
I, II, III: true.\nIV: false; $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ is less thermally stable than $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Independent check: I–III are correct: ionic hydrides release H₂ as H⁻ is oxidized; group 16 hydride stability decreases and reducing character increases down the group; interstitial hydrides are generally non-stoichiometric and retain metallic conductivity. IV is false because H₂O₂ is less thermally stable than H₂O.
solution: In ionic hydrides, $\mathrm{H^-}$ is oxidised by water, liberating $\mathrm{H_2}$; hence I is true. Down group 16, hydride thermal stability decreases while reducing character increases, and interstitial hydrides are generally non-stoichiometric and retain metallic conductivity; II and III are true. $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ is less thermally stable than $\mathrm{H_2O}$, so IV is false. Thus, I, II and III only.
